title: Pareto-optimal work extraction and the thermodynamic cost of precision in quantum information engines
authors: Jonas Berx, Ted Olander, Henning Kirchberg
abstract: We study a finite-time quantum information engine in which a two-level system is measured by a quantum harmonic oscillator acting as a meter and where useful work is extracted conditionally on the measurement outcome. Using multi-objective optimisation, we find a Pareto-optimal trade-off between extractable work and its fluctuations and show that reducing fluctuations entails higher thermodynamic costs: greater information consumption, more engine cycles, longer operation time, and reduced average work output. In the limit of a highly accurate meter, we obtain the work distribution, its moments, and the Pareto front analytically. In this regime, the work statistics of the engine reduce to those of a qubit in contact with a single thermal bath. We further analyse the associated information flows by examining the mutual information and Fisher information, and show that the Pareto-optimal engine designs lie very close to local maxima of the latter with respect to the operation time of the device. Our results provide a compact description of the trade-offs between work, its fluctuations, and thermodynamic costs in quantum information engines.
summary: This paper analyzes the trade-off between average work extraction and noise in quantum information engines using a TLS coupled to an oscillator meter. By employing multi-objective optimization and Fisher Information bounds, it shows that improving precision (reducing fluctuations) comes at a measurable thermodynamic cost. The results offer a comprehensive description of energy conversion limits governed by information theory.
main_problem: The study investigates the fundamental trade-off between maximizing extractable work and minimizing its fluctuations (precision) in a quantum information engine.
main_result: Reducing work fluctuations requires incurring higher thermodynamic costs, such as increased information consumption and longer operation times. The optimal designs are found near points where the system operates close to theoretical speed limits defined by Fisher information bounds.
method: The authors employ multi-objective optimization (Pareto front analysis) combined with deriving rigorous upper bounds on power extraction using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM).
model_or_system: The model is a finite-time quantum information engine consisting of a two-level system coupled to a quantum harmonic oscillator meter. Work is extracted conditionally based on measurement outcomes.
key_observables: Extractable Work ($\langle W_{	ext{ext}} angle$), Work Fluctuations ($\Delta W^2_{	ext{ext}}$), Mutual Information, and Fisher Information ($I(t_m)$).
important_parameters: Operation time ($t_m$), coupling strength ($g$), oscillator frequency ($\omega$), and the cold-meter limit ($\hbar\omega \gg k_B T_M$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes negligible erasure work cost for classical readout and heavily utilizes the cold meter limit to simplify calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of one engine cycle, the distribution of extracted work over multiple cycles, and plots showing optimal operating points on the Pareto front relative to speed limits derived from Fisher information.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the multi-objective optimization framework (Pareto front), then deriving analytical results for the highly accurate meter limit, and finally bounding the average power output using the Fisher Information Matrix in both general and simplified cold-meter regimes.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous thermodynamic constraint on quantum engines by linking extractable work directly to information geometry (FIM). This framework is crucial for understanding fundamental limits in measurement-based energy conversion, relevant to open quantum systems dynamics.
